name: @8bitscript/examples
description: The example programs that ship with the toolchain: hello-world, the 0.2.0 goal program, joystick, the controller test app, fancy, the raster showpiece, and swarm, the moving-objects showpiece — listed in the editor's launcher beside your own projects.

hello-world.title: Hello, World
hello-world.description: screen.blank() then text.print(0, "Hello World!") through the portable screen and text packages. The 0.2.0 goal program, and the one this toolchain is built to run first — on the PET and in the browser.

joystick.title: Joystick
joystick.description: The controller test app: a labelled map of everything @8bitscript/input exposes — UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, CONFIRM, CANCEL — with a lamp on each that flashes when that control is pressed, a running count of every press seen, and a frame counter that says the loop is live. Run it first on a machine whose input layer is new or suspect.

fancy.title: Fancy
fancy.description: The raster showpiece: a title wobbling on a sine wave inside colour bands, over @8bitscript/raster's portable per-scanline surface — the list built once, only its value bytes rewritten each frame. Everything sits behind #fact(video.raster), so the C64 and the web show the effect and the other seven machines show a static title, honestly and for free. Run before 2048 leans on the same surface.

hello-bx.title: Hello, BX
hello-bx.description: The same hello-world greeting, drawn through one 8BitX component instead of a direct text.print() call — <Hello /> elaborates to the same call at compile time, so the program is byte-identical to hello-world's own. The smallest program that shows what a .8bx file is.

swarm.title: Swarm
swarm.description: The moving-objects showpiece: sixteen sprites bouncing round the picture on a frame timeline — the title, then the sprites, then the border opens and they fly through it, then the colours rotate — through @8bitscript/sprites and @8bitscript/timeline. Hardware sprites on the C64, sixteen from eight and out into the border; a glyph per sprite on the character grid on the other eight, where what the machine cannot do folds away. The scene is one .8bx file that reads like a part list.
